\title{Modal Energy Injection in Three Fixed-Budget Contact Solvers:\\
  Measurement and a Cumulative Storage Bound}

\author{Anonymous Author(s)}

\begin{abstract}
Unilateral contact between reduced (modal) deformable bodies and rigid bodies
is commonly resolved by a velocity-level complementarity law in which one
shared multiplier couples the rigid and modal unknowns. Interactive solvers
evaluate this law under small, fixed local iteration budgets; we measure the
energetic cost of that truncation. Running one transcribed contact row through
three fixed-budget solver formulations --- position-based (XPBD),
augmented-Lagrangian (AVBD), and an implicit sequential-impulse realization ---
over an identical 24-cell scene\,$\times$\,relaxation\,$\times$\,budget sweep,
we observe behaviour that differs sharply across the three tested
implementations. Measured against the gross
rigid-side loss (a scene-wide, gravity-corrected quantity, not a per-contact
dissipation), the position-based host overdraws by up to $4.4\times10^{7}$~J
--- $1.2\times10^{5}$ times the incident rigid kinetic energy in the most
starved cells --- the augmented-Lagrangian host in $3$ of $24$ cells by at most
$6.7$~J, and the implicit realization never: a catastrophic pathology beside a
small and localized one, five orders of magnitude apart, which the customary
ratio-to-incident-energy diagnostic compresses into a single number. An iteration-budget sweep
identifies the position-based amplification as a truncation artifact, decaying
toward an implicit high-iteration reference computed in the same code path,
closing the gap
by six orders of magnitude. Since that regime is unaffordable at interactive
budgets we add a deliberately minimal fail-safe: a cumulative modal-storage
bound funded by the measured gross rigid-side loss, maintained by a reservoir
ledger and a projection of the realized modal state, whose cost we measure
rather than assume. The loop guarantees that bound unconditionally --- for any
host and any contact solve, up to a stated accounting tolerance --- and the
realized margins sit at the roundoff floor ($1.1\times10^{-13}$~J) in all 90
measured cells ($78$ distinct configurations), including the $1{\times}8$ and
$2{\times}4$ budgets at which interactive solvers are commonly deployed; what it
costs is contact validity: worst-case post-projection penetration $21.6$~mm
($72\%$ of the board's thickness) at the adversarial $4{\times}1$ corner,
$9.8$~mm at the deployed budgets.
\end{abstract}

% =====================================================================
\section{Introduction}
% =====================================================================
A deformable object that is struck at one point and rings elsewhere is
routinely modelled by projecting the elastic response onto a small modal basis.
When such a body also rests in unilateral contact with rigid bodies, the
established treatment resolves rigid and modal unknowns together through a
shared contact multiplier at the velocity level~\citep{zheng2011}. The one-way
alternative --- driving a separate modal filter from contact events without
back-reaction --- is the real-time precedent~\citep{james2002dyrt,
coevoet2020distant}. Interactive modal deformation subject to collision and
contact constraints predates both~\citep{hauser2003}.

We take this coupled row as given. Written at position level it sits one
linearization step from the velocity-level law: for a gap $C$,
$C^{n+1}\approx C^{n}+h\,\mathbf{J}\mathbf{u}^{n+1}$, which divided by $h$
recovers the velocity-level complementarity condition with a $C^{n}/h$
stabilization bias, carrying the same Jacobian and multiplier
as~\citet{zheng2011}. The row is \emph{not} a contribution of this paper, and
our transcription is narrower than the original law: modes couple through
normal rows only, and the position-level form assumes $e=0$ restitution.

Interactive solvers, however, do not solve this row to convergence: they run a
fixed, small number of local iterations per substep, and it is known that
finite-iteration coupling across a partition boundary can inject spurious
energy even when every subsystem is individually
passive~\citep{wei2026earlyterm} --- an observation that likewise predates this
work. Velocity-level frictional contact spanning rigid and reduced deformable
bodies, with the energy artifacts of iterative solvers named, goes back at
least to~\citet{kaufman2008}. What is missing is a quantitative account of this
case --- unilateral contact-to-modal transfer --- and a mitigation that fits
within an interactive budget.

\paragraph*{Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Measurement.} A single contact row evaluated in three
  fixed-budget solver implementations over one identical 24-cell adversarial
  sweep on one machine (\S\ref{sec:matrix}), plus an iteration-budget sweep
  against an implicit high-iteration reference identifying the position-based
  injection as a truncation artifact (\S\ref{sec:kconv}).
\item \textbf{A cumulative storage bound.} A one-directional bound on the
  energy entering modal storage, funded by the measured gross rigid-side loss
  and maintained by a reservoir ledger and a projection of the realized modal
  state (\S\ref{sec:bound}). It is the simplest admissible enforcement --- a
  deliberately minimal, audited fail-safe, not a constructive contact method
  --- and it guarantees \eqref{eq:invariant} unconditionally, for any host and
  any contact solve, up to an accounting tolerance; the realized margins sit at
  the roundoff floor in all $90$ measured cells ($78$ distinct configurations).
\item \textbf{The cost of enforcement.} Post-projection contact validity
  (penetration, corrective impulse, multiplier variance, momentum), measured
  rather than assumed (\S\ref{sec:validity}).
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph*{Relation to concurrent energy-control work.}
\citet{wei2026earlyterm} guarantee discrete passivity at any finite
inner-iteration budget via Douglas--Rachford splitting in wave coordinates, but
their interfaces are \emph{bilateral} couplings, not unilateral contact, and the
guarantee is structural rather than a budgeted transfer cap.
\citet{you2026energy} modify implicit Euler to track user-specified
\emph{total}-energy targets bidirectionally, with barrier contact. Ours is
neither: a one-directional cap on what contact may deposit into modal storage,
funded by measured gross rigid-side loss and enforced by scaling realized modal
state. \citet{zobel2025unity} solve ray-traced penalty contact quasi-statically
without a shared unilateral multiplier; modes and modal derivatives have served
as a \emph{deformation} surrogate in a position-based
host~\citep{peng2024reduced}, whereas here modal amplitudes enter as contact
DOFs driven by the shared multiplier.

\paragraph*{Relation to passivity control and energy projection.} The governor
transplants an established control idea rather than inventing one. Time-domain
passivity control~\citep{hannaford2002} damps once an energy observer goes
negative; energy-tank formulations~\citep{franken2011} give that observer
explicit state, so a controller spends only what its tank holds;
\citet{rath2008} enforces exact per-interface energy stability for contacting
modal objects at audio rate, where we cap a scene-level scalar reservoir. We
keep that structure and change two things: the tank is funded by \emph{measured
gross rigid-side loss}, not by the port it regulates, and the actuator scales
realized \emph{state} rather than modulating a force, because a fixed-budget
solver commits its multipliers before the excess is observable.
FEPR~\citep{dinev2018fepr} also projects state post-solve, but onto
\emph{total}-energy conservation; ours is one-sided and never restores energy
the solver lost.

% =====================================================================
\section{The row and the cumulative bound}
\label{sec:bound}
% =====================================================================
Let $\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{r}$ be mass-normalized modal amplitudes of the
supporting body, so its modal mechanical energy is
$\Emod=\tfrac12\dot{\mathbf{q}}^{\!\top}\dot{\mathbf{q}}
      +\tfrac12\mathbf{q}^{\!\top}\mathbf{K}\mathbf{q}$.
A support-contact row between a rigid corner at world height $y_c$ and the
deformed surface has gap
\begin{equation}
C \;=\; y_c \;-\; \bigl(y_{\mathrm{rest}} + \mathbf{U}_y^{\!\top}\mathbf{q}\bigr),
\qquad C \ge 0,\; \lambda \ge 0,\; C\lambda = 0,
\label{eq:row}
\end{equation}
with $\partial C/\partial\mathbf{q}=-\mathbf{U}_y$, so one multiplier $\lambda$
drives both the rigid body and the modal amplitudes. Equation~\eqref{eq:row} is
the transcription discussed above, not a new law. It is one row \emph{law},
instantiated at every support contact every substep --- $48$ such rows on the
shelf, $40$ on the ledge, $200$ on the table --- all sharing the one modal
state $\mathbf{q}$.

\paragraph*{The invariant.} We require that the energy \emph{stored in the
modal subsystem} never exceed the \emph{measured gross rigid-side loss} ---
defined exactly at \eqref{eq:derig} below --- cumulatively over the run:
\begin{equation}
\Emod^{\,n} - \Emod^{\,0}
\;\;\le\;\;
\eta \sum_{k\le n} \max\!\bigl(\dErig^{\,k},\,0\bigr),
\qquad \eta\in(0,1].
\label{eq:invariant}
\end{equation}
The transfer efficiency $\eta$ sets how much of the measured loss may be spent;
\emph{every experiment in this paper runs $\eta=1$}, the least restrictive
admissible value, so no result below depends on tuning it. The bound is
\emph{cumulative}, not per-step: a substep may deposit more than it earns
provided the running total remains within the budget, which is what lets a
legitimate ring persist across substeps.

\paragraph*{Definitions.} Modal storage is the mechanical energy of the
reduced state as written above, and $\Emod^{\,0}=0$: every scene starts from an
undeformed, resting support, so even the run's own settling transient must be
funded by the reservoir. The supply is
\begin{equation}
\dErig^{\,k} \;=\; \bigl(E_{\mathrm{rig}}^{k,-} - E_{\mathrm{rig}}^{k,+}\bigr)
                 \;+\; W_g^{\,k},
\qquad
W_g^{\,k}=\sum_b m_b\,\mathbf{g}\!\cdot\!\bigl(\mathbf{x}_b^{k,+}-\mathbf{x}_b^{k,-}\bigr),
\label{eq:derig}
\end{equation}
where $E_{\mathrm{rig}}=\sum_b\bigl[\tfrac12 m_b\|\mathbf{v}_b\|^2
+\tfrac12\boldsymbol{\omega}_b^{\!\top}\mathbf{I}_b\boldsymbol{\omega}_b\bigr]$
is \emph{purely kinetic} --- translational and rotational, over all dynamic
bodies, not merely those in contact --- and $\pm$ denote the two ends of substep
$k$. We call this the \textbf{measured gross rigid-side loss}: the scene-wide,
gravity-corrected, gross kinetic-energy loss of the rigid subsystem. It is a
\emph{loss}, not a dissipation --- it also counts legitimate rigid-to-modal
transfer and losses at rigid--rigid contacts elsewhere in the scene --- so it is
an envelope on what contact dissipated, not a measurement of it
(\S\ref{sec:limits}). Gravity enters only through $W_g$, so free ballistic
motion registers zero supply --- a falling body's kinetic gain exactly equals
the gravity work, and only an inelastic velocity change funds the reservoir.
Substep-boundary endpoints tile the timeline exactly, so no rigid energy change
escapes the accounting.

\paragraph*{Two objects, stated once.} Conflating them is the easiest way to
misread what follows. \textbf{(i)~The printed invariant} is
\eqref{eq:invariant} exactly as written: a cumulative, gross-loss-funded storage
ceiling on the modal subsystem whose supply is \emph{measured, not prescribed}
--- the right-hand side is the measured loss of \eqref{eq:derig}, never a tuned
constant or a fraction of incident energy. It is not contact-port passivity and
not a signed per-interface transfer bound: it constrains a scalar reservoir, not
a port. The \emph{gross} sum ignores substeps in which the rigid subsystem
\emph{gains} energy, so those cannot cancel earlier credits, and energy returned
and re-dissipated counts as fresh supply (\S\ref{sec:limits} measures both).
\textbf{(ii)~The enforced recursion} is the per-substep loop below --- credit,
test, project, debit --- and it maintains \eqref{eq:invariant} exactly, not a
relaxation of it: because the reservoir is credited \emph{before} the projection
test, the same-substep deposit that funds a legitimate rise in modal energy is
already inside the budget the test enforces, so no granularity slack is
required. Proposition~\ref{prop:guarantee} proves this; the only give is a
per-substep accounting tolerance, which the governed runs realize at the
$10^{-13}$~J roundoff floor.

\paragraph*{Enforcement.} A reservoir $B$ accumulates the supply and is debited
by realized storage. Both happen \emph{after} the contact solve, within the
same substep: $\dErig$ is not observable until the velocity solve
has finalized the rigid velocities, so the substep credits
$B \leftarrow B + \eta\max(\dErig,0)$ at that point, tests the realized modal
energy against it, and only then debits
$B \leftarrow \max(B - \max(\Delta\Emod,0),\,0)$. If
the realized modal energy would overdraw $B$, the state is projected onto the
admissible set by a single scalar,
\begin{equation}
(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) \;\leftarrow\; \gamma\,(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}),
\qquad
\gamma \;=\; \min\!\left(1,\;
  \sqrt{\frac{\Emod^{-} + B}{\Emod^{+}}}\right),
\label{eq:gamma}
\end{equation}
with $\Emod^{\mp}$ the modal energy before and after the solve. One substep of
the governed loop, identical in all three hosts, then reads:
{\footnotesize\emph{(1)}~snapshot $E_{\mathrm{rig}}^{-}$ (pure KE, all bodies),
$\Emod^{-}$, $\mathbf{x}^{-}$; \emph{(2)}~predict (gravity), generate contacts
at the predicted pose; \emph{(3)}~position solve ($K$ iterations), then velocity
solve --- \emph{the contact solve}; \emph{(4)}~form
$\dErig=(E_{\mathrm{rig}}^{-}\!-\!E_{\mathrm{rig}}^{+})+W_g$, i.e.\
\eqref{eq:derig}, post-solve; \emph{(5)}~credit
$B \leftarrow B + \eta\max(\dErig,0)$, same substep; \emph{(6)}~if
$\Emod^{+} > \Emod^{-} + B$, scale the state by $\gamma$ of \eqref{eq:gamma};
\emph{(7)}~debit $B \leftarrow \max(B-\max(\Delta\Emod,0),\,0)$ --- contact is
\textbf{not} re-solved.\par}
The form \eqref{eq:gamma} is closed because $\Emod$ is quadratic in the state:
scaling $\mathbf{q}$ and $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$ together scales both the kinetic
and the elastic term by $\gamma^2$, so $\gamma$ bounds the total energy rather
than the velocity alone. Two consequences are measured below: the projection
is inert whenever the solve is within budget ($\gamma=1$, bitwise-identical
trajectories), and it never re-solves contact (step~7).

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:guarantee}
For any $\eta\in(0,1]$ and any host, the loop maintains $B\ge0$ and guarantees
\eqref{eq:invariant} unconditionally, assuming nothing about the contact solve,
up to an accounting tolerance $n\epsilon$ over $n$ substeps ($\epsilon$ the
per-test tolerance, $10^{-12}$~J).
\end{proposition}

\noindent\emph{Proof.} Write $c_k=\eta\max(\dErig^{\,k},0)$ for the substep
credit and $B_k$ for the reservoir after substep $k$, and carry two invariants:
$B_k\ge0$ and $(\Emod^{k}-\Emod^{0})+B_k\le\sum_{j\le k}c_j$. Both hold at
$k{=}0$ ($B_0=\Emod^{0}=0$). The credit (step~5) enters $B$ \emph{before} the
test, so step~6 applies the largest $\gamma$ with
$\gamma^{2}\Emod^{+}\le\Emod^{-}+B_{k-1}+c_k$; as $\Emod$ is quadratic in the
state, realized storage is at most $\Emod^{-}+B_{k-1}+c_k$, i.e.\ the realized
gain $\Delta\Emod\le B_{k-1}+c_k$. The debit (step~7) sets
$B_k=\max(B_{k-1}+c_k-\max(\Delta\Emod,0),\,0)$, keeping $B_k\ge0$; and in either
branch $(\Emod^{k}-\Emod^{0})+B_k\le(\Emod^{k-1}-\Emod^{0})+B_{k-1}+c_k$, so the
second invariant follows by induction. Since $B_n\ge0$, this is
$\Emod^{n}-\Emod^{0}\le\sum_{k\le n}c_k$ --- \eqref{eq:invariant} itself, not a
relaxation: the same-substep credit absorbs the granularity term a naive
telescoping would otherwise leave. The $90$ governed cells confirm it at the
roundoff floor, worst margin $1.1\times10^{-13}$~J.

\section{Results}
% =====================================================================
All solver-behaviour measurements below come from a single machine
(Table~\ref{tab:solvers}), the sole exception being the device-resident timings
of \S\ref{sec:cost} (NVIDIA RTX 4090), reported separately; every number is
frozen with its generating command and commit hash in the supplemental ledger.
We deliberately avoid mixing machines: chaotic contact stacks diverge across
architectures under floating-point reassociation.

\subsection{One row, three implementations, the same 24 cells}
\label{sec:matrix}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering

peak modal energy / peak incident rigid kinetic energy, log scale diverging at
$1$ --- a severity diagnostic. XPBD exceeds $1$ in $8/24$ cells, AVBD in
$2/24$, the implicit realization in $0/24$. \textbf{Bottom:} the invariant
itself --- the signed margin of \eqref{eq:invariant} in joules, symmetric-log,
diverging at $0$; positive values violate. The two panels disagree on AVBD.
Hatched rows mark a relaxation axis the host does not consume, bit-identical

\end{figure*}

We drive an impactor into a modally reduced support in three scenes --- a shelf
board, a ledge slab, and a $2.2\times1.1$~m table, the last two following the
layouts of \citet{coevoet2020distant} --- and sweep modal relaxation and the
local budget (iterations $\times$ substeps) over
$\{4{\times}1, 8{\times}2, 16{\times}4, 32{\times}8\}$. The hosts are
XPBD~\citep{macklin2016xpbd}, AVBD~\citep{giles2025avbd} (a descendant of vertex
block descent~\citep{chen2024vbd}), and a sequential-impulse realization in the
sense of~\citet{catto2005iterative}, made implicit in the modal block.
Table~\ref{tab:solvers} lists what differs and what is pinned identical. Two
entries deserve emphasis. Relaxation is \emph{inert} on the impulse host --- its
implicit modal weight needs no under-relaxation and the attribute is never read,
hence the bit-identical hatched rows of Fig.~\ref{fig:matrix}. Warm start also
differs, and we run each host as published: $\lambda\!\leftarrow\!0$ every
substep is the position-based host's own form and carried duals with a growing
penalty are constitutive of the augmented-Lagrangian method, so neither is our
choice. The comparison is as-deployed, not compliance-matched.

\paragraph*{Equal row evaluations, unequal outcome.} A cell costs $K\!\cdot\!S$
row evaluations per frame, so the budget axis spans $\times64$ and conflates two
refinements that are neither interchangeable nor equally priced (a substep also
repeats contact generation and integration). At $32$ row evaluations on the
shelf drop, spent as iterations ($K{=}32,S{=}1$) the ratio is $0.300$ and
\eqref{eq:invariant} holds; spent as substeps ($K{=}4,S{=}8$) it is $3.13$,
overdrawing by $481$~J: substep refinement alone does not converge the row.

Figure~\ref{fig:matrix} shows the outcome. The position-based host exceeds
$R=1$ in $8$ of $24$ cells, worst case $1.19534\times10^{5}$ (ledge, relaxation
$1.0$, $4{\times}1$: peak modal energy $4.44\times10^{7}$~J against an incident
$371$~J); the augmented-Lagrangian host in $2$ of $24$ --- both at the starved
$4{\times}1$ corner of the table scene, worst $1.70$ --- so it is not
unconditionally benign either. The ordering is scene-dependent and it inverts:
worst-over-scenes at $4{\times}1$ the position-based host is five orders of
magnitude more energetic ($1.2\times10^{5}$ vs $1.70$), yet on the table scene
itself the augmented-Lagrangian host is the worse ($1.18$ and $1.70$ against a
position-based worst of $0.37$). Neither host dominates across scenes.

\paragraph*{The ratio is not the invariant.} An impactor's incident kinetic
energy is not the supply \eqref{eq:invariant} budgets against, so we measure
\eqref{eq:invariant} directly on all three hosts, ungoverned, running the
reservoir accounting live while forcing $\gamma\equiv1$: every state write in
the enforcement path is guarded by $\gamma<1$, so the trajectory is
bit-identical to an ungoverned run (the ratios above reproduce the independent
sweep exactly). We report the signed margin of \eqref{eq:invariant} in joules;
positive values violate. The invariant and the ratio do not flag the same
cells: the position-based host violates \eqref{eq:invariant} in $9$ of $24$
cells against $R>1$ in $8$, the augmented-Lagrangian host in $3$ against $2$,
and the implicit host in neither ($0/24$, worst margin at the roundoff floor).
Each metric catches a cell the other misses, so neither subsumes the other.
What orders the failures is magnitude: the position-based overdraw reaches
$4.4\times10^{7}$~J, five orders past the largest augmented-Lagrangian one
($6.7$~J, at the starved $4{\times}1$ table corner where $R=1.70$), itself past
the implicit host's exact zero --- three regimes the ratio-to-incident-energy
diagnostic compresses into a single number.

With enforcement enabled, all $72$ cells \emph{of this sweep} satisfy
\eqref{eq:invariant} --- $60$ of them distinct configurations, the implicit
host's $12$ relaxation pairs being bit-identical (Fig.~\ref{fig:matrix}); the
$18$ deployed-budget cells of \S\ref{sec:kconv} satisfy it too. The worst
realized ratio falls to $1.22$ (XPBD) and $0.87$ (AVBD), and the projection
never activates in any impulse cell, nor at $16{\times}4$ or $32{\times}8$ on
the position-based host at relaxation $0.7$: it is inert precisely where the
solve is already within budget.


\subsection{The position-based amplification is a truncation artifact}
\label{sec:kconv}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.88\columnwidth]{fig_s2_kconvergence.pdf}
\caption{Energy ratio versus local iteration budget $K$ on a deterministic
shelf drop, substeps pinned at $1$ so $K$ is the only variable, governor OFF.
The position-based host decays monotonically toward the implicit reference,
crossing the incident-energy threshold between $K{=}16$ and
$K{=}24$; the gap shrinks by six orders of magnitude. The
reference is the implicit realization at $K{=}500$ --- the same code path, not
a different model; it is already converged at $K{=}2$. The
AVBD curve is shown for completeness only: its denominator is itself
budget-dependent at small $K$, so it cannot be read as a convergence trend.}
\label{fig:kconv}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:kconv} isolates the local iteration budget. Two references
recur below and are not the same object: \emph{the implicit reference} is the
implicit high-iteration realization at $K{=}500$ --- the same code path run to
$K{=}500$ --- and \emph{the XPBD self-reference} is the position-based host run
to $K{=}500$ against itself. The position-based
host falls monotonically from $2.96\times10^{4}$ at $K{=}1$ to $0.300$ at
$K{=}32$, approaching the implicit reference $0.2735$; the gap
$|\text{XPBD}-\text{reference}|$ shrinks from $2.96\times10^{4}$ to
$2.7\times10^{-2}$. The implicit realization moves only in the fourth decimal
across $K=2\ldots500$ (max$-$min $6.8\times10^{-4}$).

A falling energy ratio does not by itself show that the \emph{row} is
converging --- a single scalar could shrink coincidentally. Measuring the
constraint directly resolves the question, and the two complementarity
conditions must be read in their own units rather than compounded into one
dimensionally mixed scalar. End-of-substep penetration falls from $27.9$~mm at
$K{=}1$ to $3.6\,\mu$m by $K{=}64$, where it saturates. The multiplier
surviving on \emph{separated} rows --- force where the gap is open, in units of
the steady-state median --- instead \emph{rises} from $84\times$ to $139\times$
through $K{=}24$, collapsing to exactly zero only at $K{=}64$. The energy
crossing at $K\approx24$ therefore coincides with the \emph{gap} converging,
not with complementarity holding: the multiplier side clears a rung later.
Position-based host only --- the augmented-Lagrangian multiplier is not the
same object, and the implicit realization is converged at $K{=}2$.

\paragraph*{Self-convergence stops short of the reference.} Running the
position-based host to $K\!=\!500$ against itself does not close the gap: its
ratio plateaus by $K\approx64$ at $0.2996$, so the residual $2.6\times10^{-2}$
against the reference's $0.2735$ is a fixed point, not a tail. The state agrees
no better --- on the deflection trajectory
$d_i(t)=\mathbf{U}_y[i]^{\!\top}\mathbf{q}(t)$ the peak matches to $2.4\%$ but
the trajectories differ by $6.8$~mm, $34\%$ of the reference's own peak. The two
hosts converge to different discrete solutions, as expected when they discretize
the same continuous law differently: the sweep thus separates a truncation
pathology that convergence removes from a discretization difference that it does
not.

This cuts two ways: truncation creates the amplification and convergence largely
cures it, so iterating further --- or adopting the implicit realization --- would
remove it outright, and the bound of \S\ref{sec:bound} is not a substitute for
convergence but targets the regime where neither escape is available. Following the one-iteration small-step
regime~\citep{macklin2019small}, interactive position-based solvers run
schedules near $1{\times}8$ to $2{\times}4$, well below the $K\!\ge\!24$ this
scene needs. On $18$ further cells (3 scenes $\times$ 3 hosts $\times$
$\{1{\times}8, 2{\times}4\}$, relaxation $0.7$) the position-based host violates
\eqref{eq:invariant} in all six of its deployed cells, worst $R=2282$ --- on $8$
row evaluations, twice the $4$ of the $4{\times}1$ corner --- while the others
behave as in the sweep ($1/6$ and $0/6$, the former by at most $0.011$~J).
Governed, all $18$ satisfy \eqref{eq:invariant} (worst $R = 1.023$) and the
projection is gentler: worst penetration $9.8$~mm against $21.6$.

\paragraph*{Not a knife-edge configuration.} Varying one setting at a time away
from the two worst cells --- $h$, contact and support compliance, modal rank,
both Rayleigh coefficients --- \eqref{eq:invariant} is violated with $R>1$ in
all $24$ configurations, $R$ spanning $2.5$ to $4.7\times10^{5}$. Rank localizes
the effect without removing it: excluding the stiff cluster outright (shelf
$r{=}10$) cuts $R$ from $6333$ to $22.1$, yet $584$~J is still overdrawn.
Convergence cures the worst cell as it does the shelf drop: at ledge relaxation
$1.0$, $R$ falls $8.5\times10^{5}\to0.165$ over $K{=}1\ldots32$.

\subsection{The cost of enforcement}
\label{sec:validity}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\footnotesize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\caption{Post-projection contact validity for the \emph{position-based} host at
starved budgets, relaxation $0.7$, per clamp-active substep. Gap violation is
measured immediately after the $\gamma$-scale; the corrective impulse is the
next substep's normal impulse against the unclamped steady-state median, a ratio
because the hosts' multipliers are different objects. The $4{\times}1$ cells
clamp on nearly every substep, so no steady state exists there (---).}
\label{tab:validity}
\begin{tabular}{llrrrr}
\toprule
scene & budget & clamped & gap viol.\ med / max [mm] & impulse & $\lambda$ var. \\
\midrule
shelf & $4{\times}1$ & 107/108 & 1.24 / \textbf{21.6} & ---          & --- \\
shelf & $8{\times}2$ & 171/216 & 0.21 / 6.43          & $3.68\times$ & $5.6\times$ \\
ledge & $4{\times}1$ & 97/108  & 0.08 / \textbf{21.2} & $1.03\times$ & $1.08\times$ \\
ledge & $8{\times}2$ & 178/216 & 0.07 / 4.08          & $8.92\times$ & $62\times$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph*{Accuracy.} Bounding the energy is useful only if the bounded
solution improves on the unbounded one. At a moderate injecting cell (shelf,
$8{\times}2$, relaxation $0.7$), peak modal energy is $1555.6$~J ungoverned and
$29.56$~J governed against the implicit reference's $7.92$~J: the energy error
falls $196{\times}\to3.7{\times}$ ($+1548\to+22$~J), and
$189{\times}\to3.6{\times}$ against the XPBD self-reference ($8.22$~J), so it
does not depend on the reference chosen. The trajectory, however, degrades:
$\|d-d^{\text{ref}}\|_\infty$ is $6.5$~mm ungoverned and $14.2$~mm governed,
$33\%$ and $71\%$ of the reference's peak --- the governor is a safety envelope,
not an accuracy device. At the deployed $1{\times}8$ cell energy gives
$2823{\times}\to3.7{\times}$ and the trajectory improves too ($108\to96\%$ of
reference peak): the trade is budget-dependent, but $96\%$ is still not
faithful. The $500{\times}1$ reference is converged in iteration count, not
schedule-matched to the governed $S{>}1$ runs, so the residual bounds the
governed error rather than isolating truncation from schedule mismatch.

This also explains how a $196\times$ energy error can coexist with a peak
deflection only $1.2\times$ too large: the excess is neither kinetic ($0.3\%$)
nor low-frequency --- the shelf spectrum is bimodal (ten bending modes below
$2.1$~kHz, six stiff above $20$~kHz) and $99.6\%$ of the ungoverned energy sits
in the stiff cluster, ${\sim}200\times$ the substep rate, against $0.0\%$ for
both references. A single scalar cannot redistribute energy across the spectrum:
$\gamma$ corrects the \emph{amount} ($1555.6\to29.3$~J), leaves the character
intact ($99.6\to97.7\%$), and scales the legitimate sag down with the noise
($24.1\to5.9$~mm against $20.0$).

\paragraph*{Contact validity.}
Since $\gamma<1$ shrinks the sag $\mathbf{U}_y^{\!\top}\mathbf{q}$,
\eqref{eq:gamma} lifts the support \emph{into} the resting body without
re-solving contact. Table~\ref{tab:validity} quantifies the consequence,
instrumented by wrappers that leave the solve unperturbed (clamp counts
reproduce the independent sweep exactly).

Median post-projection penetration is $0.07$--$1.24$~mm, but the worst case
reaches $21.6$~mm, a $3.1$--$12.5\times$ increase over its pre-scale value. The
shelf board is $30$~mm thick, so that is $72\%$ of its thickness; against the
unclamped scene at either reference (resting sag $1.7$--$2.4$~mm, peak
dynamic deflection $20.0$--$20.5$~mm) it is $9$--$13\times$ the sag and
$1.05$--$1.08\times$ the board's peak deflection: a visible interpenetration
where the projection is most load-bearing. Contact recovers in the next substep
rather
than accumulating, but that correction costs a normal impulse of up to
$8.9\times$ the steady-state value, with multiplier variance up to $62\times$
higher. Net rigid linear momentum is unchanged across the projection --- exactly
zero drift, verified numerically --- in every clamp-active substep of every cell,
necessarily so since \eqref{eq:gamma} writes only modal state.

On the augmented-Lagrangian host the same instrumentation fires only at its one
materially-overdrawing cell (the starved $4{\times}1$ table corner, $+6.7$~J),
where the projection is an order of magnitude gentler: it opens $1.8$~mm against
the position-based host's $21.6$, clamps a single substep against its
near-continuous firing, and needs no measurable corrective impulse. The hosts
differ in the scale of the correction, not its character (full rows in the
supplement).

\subsection{The reduced response against a full-FEM reference}
\label{sec:gt}
Bounding the energy is likewise useful only if the bounded response is correct.
On the ledge scene we compare the reduced arm against an unreduced FEM solve on
the \emph{same} discrete operator (the reduced basis is
$\mathrm{eigsh}(\mathbf{K},\mathbf{M})$ of the operator the reference
integrates), so discretization bias cancels. The reduced-to-reference
peak-deflection ratio rises monotonically $0.38\to0.54\to0.79\to0.88$ as $h$
refines $1/120\to1/960$, plateauing near $0.9$; the residual ${\sim}10\%$ is
$k{=}24$ mode truncation on a thick slab, not a coupling error --- the ring
frequency agrees to $0.4\%$ ($78.0$ vs $78.3$~Hz). The far-field shape agrees
too: peak deflection sits at the pedestal antinode, not under the impact, and
the falloff tracks the reference at Spearman $\rho=0.89$ with no fitted
attenuation term, in the small-displacement regime.

\subsection{Runtime cost}
\label{sec:cost}
On the CPU host at $16{\times}4$, over ten repetitions of $100$ frames, the
baseline step costs $11.0$--$125.6$~ms by scene and host, and the ledger adds
$0.23$--$0.41$~ms --- $0.9$--$3.4\%$ --- on the four shelf and ledge
configurations, where it resolves above run-to-run variance. On the table scene
it does not: the overhead's per-repetition spread exceeds its mean in both hosts
($+1.35\pm2.08$ and $+0.04\pm1.43$~ms), so we report it only as bounded by
${\sim}1.4$~ms. The percentage is the portable quantity: on a second machine
absolute times differ by $3.5$--$4.6\times$ while the percentages agree to within
$0.02$ points wherever both resolve. These baselines fall $1.3$--$15\times$ short
of a $120$~Hz budget, though shelf and ledge meet it at $2{\times}4$ governed.
The percentage is budget-dependent and larger at the deployed schedules: at
$1{\times}8$ and $2{\times}4$ the ledger's absolute cost stays comparable
($0.30$--$2.22$~ms) but the smaller baseline lifts it to $6.6$--$34.3\%$ (shelf
and ledge, both hosts), so enforcement is not free where the budget is tight.

A separate device-resident path (NVIDIA RTX 4090), carrying the ledger
read-only as a monitor rather than enforcing it, reaches $5.3$--$9.4$~ms/step at
$16{\times}4$ across four scenes: shelf and ledge meet a $120$~Hz budget with
margin, a road slab sits at the boundary, the table does not, and all four meet
it at $16{\times}2$ or below (per-scene factors in the supplement). We make no
unqualified real-time claim, and a device-resident \emph{enforced} $\gamma$ does
not exist in this work, so governed device timings lie outside our measurements
(\S\ref{sec:limits}).

% =====================================================================
\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limits}
% =====================================================================
\textbf{Stability is not accuracy.} Where the projection is load-bearing it
opens contact violations up to $21.6$~mm and moves the trajectory \emph{away}
from the implicit reference even as it moves the energy toward it
(\S\ref{sec:validity}): bounded, not faithful, so its honest use is as a safety
envelope for budgets that would otherwise diverge, and convergence remains the
better remedy wherever affordable. A natural next mechanism scales deviations
about the quasi-static equilibrium rather than the whole state, preserving the
load-bearing sag; it is unbuilt.

\textbf{Scope of the row.} The coupling is normal-only --- friction stays
body-local, so scraping and rolling transfer lie outside it --- and the
position-level form fixes $e=0$. The bound governs modal storage only, not
energy created spuriously in rigid degrees of freedom: in the impulse
realization, box--box rows rectifying a support ring into net rigid motion, to
which the ledger is blind by design.

\textbf{The supply is a gross sum, so it can be recycled.} Energy returning from
the modes to the rigid bodies and dissipated there is credited twice. We bound
the exposure by accumulating the opposite channel,
$\sum_k\max(-\dErig^{\,k},0)$, as a fraction of the supply: $0.4$--$27\%$
(implicit), $3$--$32\%$ (position-based) --- larger than the ${\lesssim}1\%$ we
expected --- and $102$--$118\%$ on the augmented-Lagrangian host, whose rigid
subsystem gains more than it loses in every cell, the box--box rectification
above rather than a property of the bound. Tightening the envelope needs the
signed or per-interface accounting this scalar reservoir avoids. The supply also
depends on the substep \emph{partition}: a finer schedule rectifies more
fluctuation into supply, so the budget belongs to the schedule as well as the
scene.

\textbf{Coverage.} Enforcement is host-side and single-machine (CPU float64); a
device-resident governor and a validation of the \emph{governed} path against a
full-FEM reference remain future work. Three formulations, one implementation
of each; three scenes, one contact regime; the augmented-Lagrangian host still
overdraws in $3$ of $24$ cells, so any claim that descent-class solvers are
passive in this setting is an empirical statement about this sweep, not a
theorem; since the implicit host's margins sit at exactly zero under the same
accounting, that overdraft (up to $6.7$~J) is a property of the solver, not the
ledger.

% =====================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
% =====================================================================
Transcribing an established rigid--modal contact law into fixed-budget solvers
is not energy-safe, and how unsafe differs sharply across the three tested
implementations: worst-case modal-to-incident ratios are $1.2\times10^{5}$,
$1.70$ and $0.53$ on the same 24 cells. The position-based amplification is a
truncation artifact convergence removes; the augmented-Lagrangian overdraft we
measure but do not explain. Where convergence is unaffordable, a cumulative
storage bound funded by measured gross rigid-side loss holds in every measured
cell, at a quantified cost to contact validity.
